text.p: Kenya has announced an ambitious privatisation plan for state-owned Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (KPTC), officials said on Friday.
The officials, quoting a statement from transport minister Wilson Ndolo Ayah, told Reuters the plan involves splitting the giant state enterprise into three separate entities.
The move will see the company broken split into a regulatory body, a posts division and a telecommunications service. The officials did not say when the move would be effected.
"The overall government objective for the sector is to ensure the availability of efficient, reliable and affordable communications services throughout the country," Ayah's statement said.
The government will have to amend the existing monopoly telecommunications act for the proposed changes to take effect, the officials added.
The new plan envisages the government retaining its monopoly on delivering letters and the printing and issuing of stamps.
The government has estimated a total cost of $5.4 billion which it hopes to raise through joint ventures and a public share offering on the Nairobi Stock Exchange.

"It will be very difficult for KPTC in its present structure to raise this capital on its own, which is why we are undertaking a step-by-step liberalization of the sector in order to attract capital from the private sector," the minister's statement said.
Critics say Kenya's telecommunications system is both inefficient and very expensive. In some parts of the capital Nairobi it takes up to 30 minutes to obtain a dialling tone on the phone.

On Friday, the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) which is the only global U.N. agency based in the developing world, signed a deal with Kenya for a new advanced satellite telecommunications system that will cut costs and improve the agency's information network.
UNEP officials have frequently complained that phones at their Nairobi headquarters barely functioned half the time.
The new system will provide guaranteed delivery and access to environmental data without congestion experienced on the Kenyan network.
It will also cut UNEP's annual KPTC phone bill, estimated at $5 million by half, officials said.
